title: An Architecture Search Framework for Inference-Time Techniques
summary: ARCHON automatically searches for optimal combinations of inference-time techniques (ensembling, fusion, ranking, critiquing) across multiple LLMs to outperform frontier models by 15.1% on average.
thesis: What if, instead of asking one AI model a question, you built a small assembly line of models that each play a different role — one generates answers, another critiques them, another ranks them, another merges the best parts into one final response? This paper shows a system built that way can outperform even the best single frontier model, without retraining anything, just by orchestrating existing models more cleverly. The clever part is that instead of hand-designing which roles to use and how many of each, they use an automated search to find a near-optimal combination for a given task and compute budget. The catch, which the authors are upfront about, is that all this extra machinery costs real money and time — you're making dozens of model calls instead of one, so it's a genuine tradeoff between quality and cost, not a free lunch.

claims.h: Seven distinct LLM component types each serve a specific function in the pipeline
plain: The system is built out of specialized roles, like a small team: one part generates candidate answers, another critiques them, another ranks them, another merges the best ones into a single polished response, and others check the reasoning or run tests on it.
Each role does one job well, and chaining them together produces a better final answer than any single model working alone.
body: A **Generator** produces candidate responses and can be called in parallel across multiple models (ensembling) or repeatedly on one model (repeated sampling). A **Fuser** synthesizes multiple candidates into a single higher-quality response, improving performance by 8.9% on average across benchmarks.
A **Critic** lists strengths and weaknesses of each candidate to guide downstream ranking and fusion. A **Ranker** orders candidates by quality, filtering to the top-K for the next stage.

A **Verifier** checks candidate reasoning in two stages, filtering out incorrect responses before fusion. **Unit Test Generator/Evaluator** components create and score assertion-style tests, most effective for coding and reasoning tasks.

claims.h: Bayesian optimization finds near-optimal architectures far more efficiently than exhaustive or greedy search
plain: There are thousands of ways to combine these roles — how many generators, how many rounds of critique, whether to include a ranker — far too many to try by hand.
Instead of testing all of them, the system uses a smart search that finds a near-best combination while trying only a small fraction of the possibilities.
body: The **search space** is defined by six hyperparameter axes: number of generator models (1–10), samples per generator (1–5), fusion layers (1–4), fusers per layer (2–10), whether to include critic/ranker layers, and which evaluation layer to add. After removing invalid configurations, 9,576 valid combinations remain.

**Bayesian optimization** uses a Gaussian Process surrogate model and Expected Improvement acquisition function, initialized with 230–240 random samples. It finds the best architecture in 96% of searches while requiring 88.5% fewer evaluations than greedy search and 90.4% fewer than random search.

A 20% development-set sample of the target benchmark guides search, and compute constraints (token budgets, inference-call limits) are enforced by excluding violating configurations before the optimizer considers them.

claims.h: ARCHON architectures consistently outperform frontier single-call models and prior inference-time systems
plain: The best combinations this system finds beat top single models like GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet by about 15% on average across a range of benchmarks — while actually using fewer API calls and tokens than earlier multi-model systems.
body: Across MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard-Auto, MixEval, MATH, and CodeContests, the best ARCHON configurations beat GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and OpenAI o1 by an average of 15.1%. Open-source-only ARCHON exceeds the best open-source baselines by 11.2%.

ARCHON achieves these gains while using 20% fewer inference calls, 15.1% fewer input tokens, and 13.5% fewer output tokens than competing inference-time frameworks (MoA, ADAS, AFlow). Generalized architectures trained on all tasks retain 91–94% of task-specific performance on held-out domains (GPQA, MMLU, MMLU Pro).

claims.h: Optimal component combinations differ substantially by task type
plain: The best setup isn't the same for every kind of task. Writing and instruction-following benefit most from lots of critique and merging; coding benefits most from generating tons of candidates and running automated tests on them; math benefits from generating broadly at first, then quickly narrowing down to one checked answer.
body: For **instruction-following** tasks, multiple layers of critic and fusion with diverse LLMs provide the largest gains; the Ranker is particularly effective because pairwise style comparisons are well-defined.

For **coding** tasks, ensembling and fusion alone have limited impact because one or two models dominate. Adding unit test generation/evaluation with high sample counts (up to 1000) yields a 56% boost in Pass@1 on CodeContests.
For **math** tasks, architectures favor a broad initial generation layer followed by rapid reduction to a single answer via verifier filtering, rather than iterative critique-and-fuse cycles.

claims.h: ARCHON's gains come with significant latency and cost increases that the authors acknowledge openly
plain: Running this system costs real money and time — around 30-40 separate model calls per question instead of just one, making it roughly 5 times slower and more expensive than asking a single model.
It also only works well with larger, more capable models; smaller models aren't good enough at the critique and merging roles to make the extra machinery worth it.
body: Running a full ARCHON architecture requires roughly 32–44 LLM API calls per query versus 1 for a single-model baseline, resulting in approximately 5× higher latency and cost. Per-query costs range from $0.19 to $0.45 compared to $0.017–$0.056 for single frontier models.

Bayesian optimization is less effective when the inference call budget is below 20 calls, at which point greedy or random search performs comparably. The framework also performs best with 70B+ parameter models; 7B models provide only a 7.5% improvement and are poorly suited for critique and fusion roles.
The authors suggest distillation as a future direction to pack ARCHON's aggregate knowledge into a smaller, faster model for latency-sensitive applications.

concepts.plain: Normally you train a model once and just run it to get answers. Inference-time scaling means spending extra computation at answer time—running the model many times or in clever sequences—to get better results without retraining. It trades cost-per-query for higher accuracy. That tradeoff only pays off when the accuracy gain from extra calls is worth more than the extra time and money spent getting it, which is exactly the calculation this paper's search process tries to automate.
concepts.eng: Training a model shifts parameters; inference-time techniques do not alter weights. Instead they exploit the probabilistic nature of LLM sampling: drawing multiple independent samples from the output distribution and combining them statistically outperforms a single draw, analogous to ensemble averaging in classical ML. The practical caveat is that each additional LLM call multiplies API cost and latency linearly, so returns must justify that overhead. This paper's central contribution is showing that the right combination of these techniques, chosen automatically rather than by hand, adds up to more than any single technique applied alone.

concepts.plain: Instead of asking one AI model one question, you ask several different models the same question at the same time and collect all their answers. Combining diverse answers tends to be better than any single answer alone. This works because different models make different mistakes. The tradeoff is that querying several models costs more than querying one, so this only helps when the extra diversity translates into better answers often enough to justify the added expense.
concepts.eng: Ensemble diversity is the key mechanism: models trained on different data or with different architectures produce uncorrelated errors, so their combination via voting or fusion reduces variance. This mirrors classical bootstrap aggregation (bagging) but operates over discrete text outputs rather than numeric predictions. The caveat is diminishing returns—models must differ meaningfully; running the same model repeatedly adds less diversity than adding a distinct model. In this paper, ensembling is typically the first stage in a longer pipeline, feeding its diverse candidate pool into critique, ranking and fusion stages that do the actual work of picking or combining a final answer.

concepts.plain: After collecting several candidate answers, a separate language model reads all of them and writes one new, combined answer that is better than any individual response. It is not just picking the best answer—it synthesises a genuinely new one. The paper shows this consistently outperforms simply selecting the top-ranked answer. Because fusion actually reads and rewrites content rather than just choosing between existing options, it can rescue a good idea from an otherwise weak answer and combine it with a good idea from a different one.
concepts.eng: Fusion is a generative operation: the fuser LLM is conditioned on the instruction plus all candidates and must produce a response that synthesises correct elements while discarding errors, analogous to a learned combiner in stacked generalisation. It outperforms oracle selection (picking the single best candidate) because it can merge complementary correct sub-parts from different responses. The practical limit is context-window size: too many or too long candidates overflow the fuser's context, which is why the paper caps candidates at 24. This makes fusion strictly more powerful than any selection-based method in principle, at the cost of an extra LLM call whose own reliability becomes part of the system's overall error budget.

concepts.plain: Before fusing answers, a model reads each candidate and writes down what is good and bad about it (critique), and another model orders them from best to worst (ranking). These steps give the fuser better information to work with. The paper finds critics and rankers are most useful for instruction-following tasks where style and completeness matter. Skipping straight from raw candidates to fusion without these intermediate steps tends to produce a noticeably worse final answer, since the fuser has to do all the quality assessment itself in one pass.
concepts.eng: The critic acts as a structured feature extractor: converting raw text candidates into strength/weakness annotations gives the fuser explicit signals rather than forcing it to infer quality implicitly. The ranker applies pairwise comparison—a technique borrowed from learning-to-rank literature—to filter the candidate set before fusion, reducing noise. The caveat is that ranking is harder for math and coding tasks where correctness is binary and stylistic comparisons break down. Both modules exist specifically to reduce the burden on the fuser, converting an unstructured pile of candidate text into a smaller, better-labeled set the fusion stage can work with more reliably.

concepts.plain: There are thousands of possible ways to combine these AI modules, and testing every combination would be too expensive. Bayesian optimisation is a smart search method that builds a statistical model of which configurations tend to work well and uses it to guess which untested configuration to try next. It finds good architectures using far fewer trials than random or exhaustive search. This matters practically because testing every possible pipeline configuration by brute force would cost far more in API calls than the system could ever save once deployed.
concepts.eng: Bayesian optimisation maintains a Gaussian Process surrogate model over the objective surface (benchmark accuracy vs. configuration vector). An acquisition function—here Expected Improvement—balances exploration of uncertain regions against exploitation of known good regions, avoiding the combinatorial explosion of grid search. The paper reports it requires 88–90% fewer evaluations than greedy or random search, but it is less effective below ~20 inference calls because the search space is too small to benefit from the surrogate model's prior. The same surrogate-model approach is standard practice in other expensive black-box optimisation settings, like tuning neural network hyperparameters, where each individual evaluation is too costly to explore exhaustively.

concepts.plain: The set of all possible ARCHON configurations is defined by six parameters such as how many models to use and how many fusion layers to include. Not all combinations are valid—for example, too many candidates can overflow a model's memory for text. Valid configurations total about 9,576 out of a theoretical 18,750. Filtering out the invalid combinations before the search even starts keeps the optimizer from wasting evaluations on configurations that could never actually run.
concepts.eng: The configuration space X is a Cartesian product of integer and binary dimensions; invalid configurations arise from two hard constraints: exceeding the fuser's context window (capped at 24 candidates) and structural contradictions (single fusion layer cannot simultaneously have multiple fusers). Pruning invalid points before search is critical—including them would waste evaluations and could skew the surrogate model. This is directly analogous to design-space exploration in chip design where physical constraints eliminate large fractions of the nominal parameter space. Handled correctly, this pruning step is what keeps the search tractable — without it, the optimizer would burn a meaningful fraction of its limited evaluation budget on configurations doomed to fail before returning any signal.

concepts.plain: After generating answers, a separate model checks whether each answer is logically correct by first explaining why it might be right, then issuing a pass/fail verdict. Only answers that pass move forward in the pipeline. This is most useful for math and reasoning tasks where correctness can be checked step by step. Forcing the model to explain its reasoning before giving a verdict tends to catch more mistakes than just asking 'is this right, yes or no' outright.
concepts.eng: The verifier implements a two-stage chain-of-thought: stage one generates supporting reasoning (forcing the model to articulate justification before judging), stage two uses that reasoning plus the original prompt to emit a binary verdict. This reduces false positives compared to a single-pass verdict because the model must commit to an explanation first. The caveat is cost—two LLM calls per candidate—and it offers little benefit for instruction-following tasks where correctness is subjective rather than verifiable. Because it runs as a separate, explicit filtering stage, it complements rather than replaces the fuser — a wrong answer can be screened out before it ever gets a chance to contaminate a fused response.

concepts.plain: For coding and reasoning tasks, the system automatically generates a set of specific tests (like 'does the answer mention X?') and then checks each candidate answer against those tests. Candidates that pass more tests are ranked higher or allowed to continue. This extends software unit-testing ideas to general question-answering. Because the tests are written in plain language rather than code, this same trick can be applied well beyond programming problems, anywhere a candidate answer can be checked against a specific, checkable claim.
concepts.eng: The unit test generator produces natural-language assertions rather than executable code, making the approach domain-agnostic. The evaluator then applies each assertion to each candidate using LLM-based natural language inference, aggregating pass/fail scores to rank or filter responses. For coding tasks specifically, combining high sample counts with unit test filtering produced a 56% Pass@1 improvement, because the correct solution appears in at least one sample with high probability (coverage) and tests reliably identify it (precision). This generality is the key design choice: by keeping assertions in natural language rather than executable code, the same evaluation machinery works across domains without needing a code interpreter or task-specific tooling.

concepts.plain: You can search for the best pipeline configuration for one specific type of task, or for a single configuration that works reasonably well across all tasks. Task-specific configurations perform better but require separate search per task. The general-purpose configuration retains 91–94% of task-specific performance on unseen benchmarks. In practice, most real deployments don't know exactly what kind of question is coming next, which is why the paper spends real effort validating that the general-purpose option isn't a big compromise.
concepts.eng: This is the classic bias-variance tradeoff applied at the system level: task-specific architectures overfit to a benchmark's characteristics (e.g., coding prefers unit-test filtering; instruction-following prefers deep fusion) whereas the general architecture is a regularised compromise. The 20% held-out evaluation protocol guards against benchmark overfitting during architecture search. The practical implication is that a general architecture amortises search cost across many tasks at modest accuracy loss, which is the preferred operating point when query distribution is unknown. This tradeoff mirrors a familiar choice in machine learning more broadly: a specialized model always wins on its home turf, but a generalized one is what you actually want when you can't predict the distribution of incoming tasks in advance.

concepts.plain: Different tasks use different scorecards. Coding tasks use Pass@1: does the single output produced actually pass all the test cases? Instruction-following tasks use win rate: do human or AI judges prefer this model's answer over a reference model's answer? These metrics capture fundamentally different notions of quality.
concepts.eng: Pass@1 is a deterministic correctness metric drawn from competitive programming evaluation—the generated code either satisfies all hidden test cases or it does not, making it sensitive to sample efficiency. Win rate is a preference metric derived from pairwise comparison (Bradley-Terry model), which captures stylistic quality and instruction adherence that ground-truth labels cannot. The two metrics respond differently to inference-time techniques: repeated sampling with unit-test selection improves Pass@1 sharply, while fusion and critique layers improve win rate most, which is why optimal architectures differ by task type. Knowing which metric a task will be judged on is itself part of choosing the right architecture, since a pipeline tuned to maximize one can actively underperform on the other.

sections.s: ARCHON is a modular automated framework that selects and combines inference-time techniques and LLMs given a compute budget, searching a large design space to find optimized configurations. It outperforms frontier models (o1, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) by 15.1% on average while using fewer tokens than competing inference-time systems.

Inference-time techniques (ensembling, ranking, fusion, repeated sampling) improve LLM output quality but no single approach dominates across all tasks, and the search space for combining them is huge. The paper frames three challenges: understanding utility of each technique, understanding interactions between techniques, and automatically searching the large architecture space.

Prior systems like MoA, LLM-Blender, ADAS, and AFlow each address only a subset of inference-time techniques, often targeting specific benchmarks or single-LM orchestration. ARCHON unifies all techniques and automates architecture construction, distinguishing it from prompt-engineering tools like DSPy.

ARCHON defines seven LLM component types: Generator, Fuser, Critic, Ranker, Verifier, Unit Test Generator, and Unit Test Evaluator, each with defined inputs, outputs, and inference costs. Fuser alone improves performance 8.9% on average; Critic adds 11.5 points in a 10-model ensemble; Verifier is most effective on reasoning tasks.

Components must follow six ordering rules (e.g., Generators only in first layer, Critic before Ranker/Fuser) inspired by ablation studies across seven benchmarks. Key trends: more models and samples give 9.3–18.5% gains (T1), stacking technique layers helps (T2–T3), and Verifier/Unit Test modules filter bad answers in reasoning tasks (T4).

ARCHON uses Bayesian optimization over a 9,576-configuration search space defined by six hyperparameters (generators, samples, fusion layers, fusers per layer, critic/ranker flag, evaluation layer). Bayesian optimization finds the best architecture in 96% of searches, needing 88.5% fewer evaluations than greedy search and 90.4% fewer than random search.

Evaluation uses seven benchmarks spanning instruction-following (MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, Arena-Hard-Auto), reasoning (MixEval, MixEval-Hard, MATH), and coding (CodeContests), with architecture search on a 20% dev split and evaluation on the held-out 80%. Models span 8B open-source, 70B+ open-source, and closed-source APIs including GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet.

ARCHON consistently beats single-call LLMs and prior inference-time systems across all benchmarks, using 20% fewer inference calls and 15.1% fewer input tokens than MoA/ADAS/AFlow while achieving higher accuracy. Closed-source ARCHON beats o1 by 8.1% on average across the seven benchmarks.

Instruction-following benefits most from multi-layer fusion and diverse model ensembles; reasoning tasks need per-subtask architectures for maximum gains; coding benefits most from heavy repeated sampling plus unit test evaluation (56% Pass@1 boost on CodeContests). Generic ensemble+fusion architectures are less effective for coding tasks where one model dominates.

sections.h: Model Size, Latency, and Cost Discussion
sections.s: ARCHON works best with 70B+ models; 7B models are adequate for ranking but weak for critique and fusion, yielding only 7.5% gains over the best single 7B model. Latency and cost are 5x a single API call, which the authors argue is acceptable for high-value domains, with distillation as a future mitigation.

sections.h: Component Ablation Tables and Detailed Prompts
sections.s: Detailed tables (Tables 5–9) show every combination of ARCHON components across all benchmarks for open-source 70B+, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Claude Haiku, plus the exact prompts used for each component. Use these tables to understand which component combinations matter most for a given task type before deploying.

sections.h: Bayesian Optimization Details and Search Algorithm Comparison
sections.s: The search space is formally defined with six hyperparameters and 9,576 valid configurations; the objective balances accuracy and compute cost with a tunable lambda. Tables 26–27 show that 230–240 initial random samples is the sweet spot, and Bayesian optimization is inferior to greedy only for budgets under 20 inference calls.

jargon.d: Any method that uses extra computation when the model is answering a query, rather than during training. The goal is to improve output quality without retraining. This paper treats techniques like repeated sampling, ranking, and fusion as modular building blocks that can be combined into a pipeline, and studies which combinations work best for which task types.

Running several different LLMs on the same prompt simultaneously to produce a pool of candidate answers. Analogous to an ensemble in classical ML where multiple classifiers vote. ARCHON uses this as its first layer, selecting the top-K models ranked by individual benchmark performance, then passing all candidates to downstream components.

An LLM prompted to synthesize multiple candidate responses into one higher-quality output. It is not a simple vote; it reads all candidates and rewrites them. The paper finds Fuser is the single most impactful component, improving average performance by 8.9%, and stacking multiple Fuser layers further helps instruction-following tasks.

An LLM that reads all candidate responses and produces a structured critique of each, noting strengths and weaknesses. This critique text is then passed to the Fuser or Ranker to guide their decisions. Adding a Critic before fusion improved average performance by about 3.1 percentage points across all benchmarks tested.

An LLM that does pairwise comparison of candidate responses and outputs a ranked list, allowing only the top-K to proceed. Found most useful for instruction-following where style and prompt adherence matter. On MT Bench and Arena-Hard-Auto it improved selection quality by 10.8% over random selection.

jargon.h: model checking answer correctness in two stages
jargon.d: A two-pass LLM component: first it generates reasoning for why a candidate answer is correct, then it issues a binary Correct/Incorrect verdict. Only verified responses advance. Most effective on reasoning tasks, boosting MixEval and MATH by 8.4%, but less helpful for open-ended instruction-following tasks.

A global optimization method that fits a probabilistic surrogate model (here a Gaussian Process) to results of previously tested configurations, then uses an acquisition function called Expected Improvement to pick the next configuration to try. ARCHON uses it to search its 9,576-configuration architecture space, finding the best architecture in 96% of runs while requiring 88-90% fewer evaluations than random or greedy search.

jargon.h: fraction of problems solved first try
jargon.d: A coding benchmark metric: the fraction of test problems for which the model's single generated solution passes all hidden test cases on the first attempt. Used here for MATH and CodeContests. ARCHON raised CodeContests Pass@1 from 17.9% to 29.3% by adding unit test generation and heavy sampling.

A benchmark of 80 multi-turn conversational prompts judged by GPT-4 using pairwise comparison against a reference model. Scores are reported as win rates. Used in this paper as a primary instruction-following evaluation; ARCHON all-source task-specific architectures reached 79.5% win rate versus 44.2% for a single GPT-4o call.

A benchmark of 500 difficult prompts where model outputs are judged head-to-head by GPT-4-Turbo against a reference model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet or GPT-4-0314). Win rate is the fraction of queries the tested model wins. The paper reports ARCHON reaching 92.5% win rate on this benchmark with all-source task-specific configuration.

A 2000-question benchmark that mixes multiple existing evaluation datasets (GSM8K, TriviaQA, DROP, MATH, BBH, AGIEval) and scores by exact ground-truth match rather than LLM judging. MixEval-Hard is a harder 500-question subset. Used to evaluate reasoning generalization; ARCHON gains are smaller here than on chat benchmarks.

A set of 140 competition-style programming problems (image-free subset) scored by running generated code against hidden test cases (Pass@1). The paper finds standard ensembling and fusion techniques add little value here; large gains come from scaling the number of generated samples plus model-based unit test evaluation.

A family of techniques that automatically discover neural network architectures rather than designing them by hand. ARCHON borrows this concept and applies it to LLM pipelines: instead of searching layer types and widths, it searches which inference-time components to use, how many models to include, and how many layers to stack.

The metric used by chat benchmarks like MT-Bench, AlpacaEval 2.0, and Arena-Hard-Auto. A judge LLM compares the tested model's output to a reference model's output and picks a winner; win rate is the percentage of queries where the tested model wins. Length-Controlled Win Rate (L.C. W.R.) adjusts for response verbosity to avoid rewarding padding.

In Bayesian optimization, a surrogate model (here a Gaussian Process) approximates the true objective function—benchmark performance as a function of architecture hyperparameters—without running the full expensive evaluation. After each real evaluation the surrogate is updated. ARCHON uses it to predict which untested architecture configurations are likely to perform well.

context:
ARCHON (Architecture Search Framework for Inference-Time Techniques) is an open-source modular framework from Stanford and University of Washington (arXiv:2409.15254v6, June 2025) that automates the design of LLM inference-time architectures. Given a compute budget and a set of available LLMs, ARCHON uses Bayesian optimization to search a design space of 9,576 valid configurations (reduced from an initial 18,750 by removing invalid ones where initial generations exceed fuser context window of 24 candidates, or where a single fuser layer contains multiple fusers when xf=1 and xr>=2). The search hyperparameter axes are: (1) top-K generators for ensemble, range 1-10; (2) top-K generator samples per model, range 1-5 (extended to 1,10,100,500,1000 for CodeContests); (3) number of fusion layers, range 1-4; (4) number of fusers per layer, range 2-10 in steps of 2; (5) whether to use critic and ranker layers before each fuser, binary; (6) evaluation layer choice: Verifier, Unit Test Generator/Evaluator, or neither before final fuser. All LLM generation temperatures are set to 0.7. Architecture search uses 20% of each target dataset as development set, evaluating on the held-out 80%. The delta between full benchmark and held-out performance averages 0.44% with SD 0.20%.

ARCHON defines seven LLM component types. Generator: takes instruction prompt, outputs candidate responses, 1 call per candidate, all domains. Fuser: merges multiple candidates into one, 1 call per candidate, all domains. Critic: generates strengths/weaknesses for each candidate, 1 call, all domains. Ranker: returns top-K candidates by quality ranking, 1 call, all domains. Verifier: two-stage verification (stage 1 generates reasoning, stage 2 outputs binary Correct/Incorrect verdict), 2 calls per candidate, reasoning tasks. Unit Test Generator: produces 5-10 test statements from instruction prompt, 1 call, reasoning tasks. Unit Test Evaluator: scores candidates against generated tests, 1 call per candidate, reasoning tasks. Construction rules: only one component type per layer; Generators only in first layer; Critic must precede Ranker or Fuser; Ranker/Critic/Verifier/Unit Test components cannot be in the first layer and must be the sole module in their layer; multiple Fusers allowed in one layer; Unit Test Generator always immediately precedes Unit Test Evaluator.

Bayesian optimization uses Expected Improvement acquisition function with a Gaussian Process surrogate model initialized with 230-240 random samples (empirically optimal). It finds the best architecture in 96.0% of searches, requiring 88.5% fewer evaluations than greedy search and 90.4% fewer than random search. For inference budgets under 20 calls, Bayesian optimization is less effective and greedy search performs comparably. Optimal initial sample count is 230-240; beyond this, marginal returns decrease.

Key empirical trends: T1: repeated model sampling gives 9.3% gains; ensemble scaling gives 18.5% gains. T2: scaling fusion layers improves performance across task types; always adding a single fuser as the last layer helps. T3: diversity of techniques (critics and rankers before fusers) bolsters performance. T4: Verifier and Unit Test Generator/Evaluator alongside Fuser improves reasoning and coding by filtering flawed responses.

Component-level performance findings: Fuser improves performance 8.9% on average across all benchmarks; adding multiple Fuser layers gives 1-2 point gains on MixEval but 10-15 point win rate gains on MT Bench and AlpacaEval 2.0 with 3-4 layers. Ranker improves over random selection by 10.8% on MT Bench and Arena-Hard-Auto, within 2.7% of oracle. Critic improves performance 11.5 percentage points average with 10-model 70B+ ensemble plus Fuser. Verifier improves 8.4% on MixEval, MixEval Hard, and MATH; lags ensemble+fuser by 1.5% alone. Unit Test Generator/Evaluator gives 7.4% boost on reasoning/coding; alone lags ensemble+fuser by 3.1%; combined with scaling for CodeContests gives 56% Pass@1 boost from 17.9 to 29.3.

Main results (Table 1, held-out 80% subset): Single-call baselines: GPT-4o averages 18.1% CodeContests Pass@1, 83.5% MATH, 87.5% MixEval, 63.4% MixEval Hard, 80.6% Arena Hard Auto, 57.8% AlpacaEval 2.0 LC WR, 44.2% MT Bench. MoA uses 19 inference calls, 25,109 avg input tokens, 17,422 avg output tokens. ADAS uses 52 calls, 72,804 input tokens, 44,872 output tokens. AFlow uses 48 calls, 68,596 input tokens, 41,748 output tokens. o1 token counts unknown. ARCHON open-source task-specific: 44 calls, 63,157 input tokens, 39,949 output tokens; scores 71.1% MT Bench, 68.1% AlpacaEval, 89.6% Arena Hard Auto, 67.5% MixEval Hard, 88.8% MixEval, 89.5% MATH, 28.9% CodeContests. ARCHON all-source task-specific: 39 calls, 58,250 input tokens, 36,114 output tokens; scores 79.5% MT Bench, 69.0% AlpacaEval, 92.5% Arena Hard Auto, 72.7% MixEval Hard, 89.7% MixEval, 93.5% MATH, 41.4% CodeContests. ARCHON outperforms frontier models by 15.1% average; beats o1 and o1-mini by 8.1% and 9.7% respectively. Open-source ARCHON surpasses SOTA open-source by 11.2%. ARCHON uses 20.0% fewer inference calls, 15.1% fewer input tokens, and 13.5% fewer output tokens than best alternative inference-time frameworks. Generalized all-source ARCHON achieves 6.4% better performance while being 31% more token efficient than best LM system baselines. Targeted architectures use 15.5% more input and 18.6% more output tokens than generalized but achieve 8.4% higher accuracy.

Generalization results (Table 2): All-source generalized ARCHON achieves 91.7% of task-specific performance on GPQA Diamond (56.1% vs 61.2%), 93.9% on MMLU (76.5% vs 81.5%), 94.2% on MMLU Pro (71.0% vs 75.4%). Generalized ADAS achieves 73.2%/73.3%/66.8% preservation; generalized AFlow achieves 70.8%/73.8%/67.0% preservation. ARCHON framework works best with 70B+ parameter models; 7B models boost performance 7.5% over best individual 7B model but are less effective for critique and fusion. ARCHON costs approximately 5x more in time and money than a single LLM API call. Best all-source general-purpose architecture: 10 generators followed by four successive critic-ranker-fuser layers with Qwen2 72B critic and Claude 3.5 Sonnet ranker/fuser, with funneling from 8 to 6 to 4 fusers per layer. Task-specific coding architectures use multiple rounds of generation, critique, fusion, and unit testing over single responses.
